The scale shows that two grid squares represent one unit. Reading the displacements from the diagram gives

$$
q=\left\langle\frac52,-\frac32\right\rangle,
\qquad r=\left\langle\frac32,3\right\rangle.
$$

Thus $q+r=\langle4,\frac32\rangle$ and

$$
|q+r|=\sqrt{4^2+\left(\frac32\right)^2}=\frac{\sqrt{73}}2.
$$

The required unit vector is

$$
\frac{q+r}{|q+r|}=\frac{2(q+r)}{\sqrt{73}}.
$$

batches.before:
Using the worksheet’s geometric meaning of integral curve, draw the entire right branch $x^2-y^2=1/4$, $x>0$, including its turn at $(1/2,0)$. One parametrization is $(x,y)=(\tfrac12\cosh s,\tfrac12\sinh s)$. Draw its visible portion within the supplied axes. Away from $y=0$, its slope is $dy/dx=\cosh s/\sinh s=x/y$. The whole curve is not a solution graph $y(x)$: for $x>1/2$ it has two $y$ values, and the explicit ODE is undefined at its vertical tangent $(1/2,0)$.

![Authored reference graph](images/1a/1a426ad2bc023da1fc079d9ca7017c8735d1495114389a0d020cf1874195071d.png)

Here “integral curve” means a geometric trajectory following the line directions, including a vertical turn; it is broader than a classical solution graph of $y\prime=x/y$. The parametric tangent $(\tfrac12\sinh s,\tfrac12\cosh s)=(y,x)$ remains nonzero at the turn. Each upper/lower portion can separately define a solution for $x>1/2$, but their union cannot.

batches.before:
Let $g(x)=x^2-3x+3$ and rewrite the outer function as $F(u)=2u^{-1/2}$, so $f(x)=F(g(x))$.

Differentiate the outer and inner functions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F'(u)&=2\left(-\frac12\right)u^{-3/2}=-u^{-3/2}, \\
g'(x)&=2x-3.
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the chain rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)&=F'(g(x))g'(x) \\
&=-(x^2-3x+3)^{-3/2}(2x-3) \\
&=\frac{3-2x}{(x^2-3x+3)^{3/2}} \\
&=\frac{1}{(x^2-3x+3)^{3/2}}(3-2x).
\end{aligned}
$$

The missing factor is $3-2x$. It includes both the inner derivative and the outer derivative's factor of $-1$.

Since $x^2-3x+3=(x-\frac32)^2+\frac34>0$, this derivative is defined for every real $x$.

batches.before:
Let $u(x)=x^2-2x+2$ and $v(x)=x^2+x+1$. Then

$$
u'(x)=2x-2,\qquad v'(x)=2x+1.
$$

The quotient rule gives

$$
f'(x)=\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2}.
$$

Expand the two products in the numerator separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}u'(x)v(x)&=(2x-2)(x^2+x+1)\\&=2x^3+2x^2+2x-2x^2-2x-2\\&=2x^3-2,\\u(x)v'(x)&=(x^2-2x+2)(2x+1)\\&=2x^3+x^2-4x^2-2x+4x+2\\&=2x^3-3x^2+2x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtract these products and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{(2x^3-2)-(2x^3-3x^2+2x+2)}{(x^2+x+1)^2}\\&=\frac{2x^3-2-2x^3+3x^2-2x-2}{(x^2+x+1)^2}\\&=\frac{3x^2-2x-4}{(x^2+x+1)^2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The cubic terms cancel. The derivative is valid for every real $x$, since $x^2+x+1=(x+\tfrac12)^2+\tfrac34>0$.
